prompt: A project's owner tries to create a service account key, and an organisation policy forbids keys. What happens?
hint: Which of the two decides what may be done at all?

choices.text: It succeeds, as Owner outranks every policy
choices.why: IAM decides who; the policy decides what. Owner is still a who.

choices.text: It is refused, whatever the owner's role
choices.why: Right. A guardrail that a powerful role could step over would not be a guardrail.

choices.text: It succeeds and the key is deleted by the policy an hour later
choices.why: A policy refuses at creation. It never deletes anything afterwards.

choices.text: It succeeds if the owner holds `roles/iam.serviceAccountKeyAdmin` too
choices.why: No role lifts a constraint. Only changing the policy does.

prompt: What is the difference between a constraint and an organisation policy?
hint: One is defined by Google; the other is attached by you.

choices.text: They are two names for the same object
choices.why: They are two objects: the rule, and the rule applied with a value.

choices.text: A policy is a group of constraints sold as a bundle
choices.why: A policy sets exactly one constraint on one node.

choices.text: A constraint applies to IAM and a policy to networks
choices.why: Both apply wherever the constraint's subject is, IAM and networks among many.

choices.text: A constraint is a rule; a policy sets it on a node
choices.why: Right. `gcp.resourceLocations` does nothing until a policy gives it values somewhere in the tree.

prompt: Match each kind of constraint to an example of it.
hint: On or off; a list; a condition.

pairs.right: a CEL condition on a firewall rule's fields

right_distractors: a role granted on a folder

prompt: A location policy allowing only South America is enforced on Monday. A disk created in Iowa last year is still there on Tuesday. Why?

choices.text: It is checked at creation, not afterwards
choices.why: Right. Turning one on is the moment to look for what it would have refused.

choices.text: Policies take a week to propagate
choices.why: They take effect within minutes, and still never touch what already exists.

choices.text: Disks are exempt from location policies
choices.why: A new disk in Iowa would be refused. The old one predates the policy.

choices.text: The disk's project overrides the organisation's policy
choices.why: Nothing says the project wrote a policy. The reason is the date.

prompt: `in:southamerica-locations` is a value ___, which names every region and zone in South America at once.
Why is the role to set organisation policies kept separate from Owner and held on the organisation?
hint: What would a project owner do with it?

choices.text: Because policies are billed to the organisation
choices.why: Policies cost nothing. The separation is about who decides.

choices.text: Because Owner cannot be granted on a folder
choices.why: Owner can be granted on a folder. That is unrelated to policies.

choices.text: So owners cannot override the guardrails
choices.why: Right. If owners wrote their own policies, every guardrail would be one override away from gone.

choices.text: Because a policy needs the organisation's billing account
choices.why: Policies have nothing to do with billing.

prompt: The organisation allows `in:southamerica-locations` and `in:us-locations`. A folder sets `in:southamerica-east1-locations` with `inherit_from_parent = true`. Where may its projects create resources?
hint: Inheriting an allow list merges it.

choices.text: In São Paulo only
choices.why: That would need the folder to replace, not inherit.

choices.text: Nowhere, as the two values conflict
choices.why: Allowed values merge without conflict; the union is the answer.

choices.text: In South America or the United States
choices.why: Right. The folder's value is added to the parent's, so nothing became stricter.

choices.text: In the United States only, the parent's last value
choices.why: Order means nothing here. The merged list holds every value.

prompt: The organisation sets the boolean `compute.requireOsLogin` on. A project sets it off. What is the project's effective policy?
hint: A boolean has nothing to merge.

choices.text: Off: the nearest policy wins
choices.why: Right. Which is why setting policies is a role on the organisation and nowhere else.

choices.text: On: the organisation always wins
choices.why: For a boolean, the closest node's policy is the answer.

choices.text: Both, merged into a dry run
choices.why: Dry run is a separate policy somebody writes; nothing turns into one by conflict.

choices.text: Undefined until somebody resets it
choices.why: The answer is well defined: the nearer policy.

prompt: What does `reset = true` on a folder's policy do?

choices.text: It deletes the policy on the organisation
choices.why: It changes the answer for the folder and below, and touches nothing above.

choices.text: It re-reads the parent's policy
choices.why: That is plain inheritance. Reset ignores the parent.

choices.text: It removes every resource that breaks the policy
choices.why: Policies never remove resources, reset included.

choices.text: It returns to the constraint's default, Google's
choices.why: Right. As if no policy existed above the folder.

prompt: A team wants to forbid service account keys but fears it will break a nightly job nobody remembers. What does Google recommend?
hint: There is a way to see refusals without refusing.

choices.text: Enforce it on a Friday and revert if somebody complains
choices.why: That finds the job by breaking it. A dry run finds it without the outage.

choices.text: A dry run, then read the audit log of what it would have refused
choices.why: Right. A week of violations names the job, and the team fixes it before enforcing.

choices.text: Enforce it, since policies are not retroactive and the job's key stays
choices.why: Existing keys stay, but a job that creates keys would start failing. The fear is reasonable.

choices.text: Grant the job's account Owner so the policy skips it
choices.why: No role lifts a constraint, and Owner on a job is a second problem.

prompt: Put the steps of introducing a risky guardrail in the order Google recommends.
items: write the policy as a dry run
read the violations in the audit log
fix or exempt what deserves it
trap: Enforcing before reading the violations is the slip: the dry run is only useful if somebody looks at what it found.

prompt: Why does `policies.tf` write `inherit_from_parent = false` on production when false is the default?
hint: A default is invisible; a written line is a decision on the page.

choices.text: To make the decision visible to whoever reads it next
choices.why: Right. Somebody setting it to true would have to delete a deliberate line first.

choices.text: Without it, Terraform would refuse the policy
choices.why: The provider accepts the policy without the line; the plan would be the same.

choices.text: Without it, the folder would merge with the organisation
choices.why: False is the default, so leaving it out also replaces. The line documents, it does not change.

choices.text: It makes the policy a dry run
choices.why: A dry run is `dry_run_spec`, a different block.

choices.text: The policies as Google holds them today
choices.why: Nothing here asked Google. The file is Terraform's own plan.

choices.text: The effective policy of every project
choices.why: Effective policies are computed by Google's service, which no plan consults.

choices.text: The saved plan, as JSON
choices.why: Right. `jq` then picks the fields worth reading out of it.

choices.text: The audit log of the dry run
choices.why: Violations land in Google's audit logs, after an apply. A plan has none.

prompt: The plan for `policies.tf` passes. Applied in a real organisation by somebody holding only Owner on `planner-dev`, what happens?
hint: Where must the role to set policies be held?

choices.text: The three policies are created, since the plan passed
choices.why: A plan checks the description, never the caller's roles.

choices.text: Refused: it takes `roles/orgpolicy.policyAdmin` on the organisation
choices.why: Right. Owner of one project grants nothing on the organisation, and the plan could not see that.

choices.text: Only the policy on `planner-dev` is created
choices.why: None of the three is on `planner-dev`; they are on the organisation and a folder.

choices.text: The dry run is created and the other two are refused
choices.why: A dry run is a policy like the others and needs the same role.

prompt: How many organisation policies does the plan for `policies.tf` add?
Customers' data must stay in Brazil. The organisation allows South America and the United States. A new folder `customer-data` should allow only São Paulo. Which policy on the folder does it?
hint: For an allow list, what does inheriting do?

choices.text: Its own list, inheriting from the organisation
choices.why: Inheriting would add São Paulo to the parent's list and keep the United States.

choices.text: A `reset`, so Google's default applies
choices.why: Google's default for locations allows everywhere, the opposite of the intention.

choices.text: No policy, and a label `residency=br` on each project
choices.why: A label decides nothing, and anybody who edits the project can change it.

choices.text: Its own list, not inheriting
choices.why: Right. Replacing makes São Paulo the whole answer for the folder and below.
